guideTitle: 6 Best Drop Arm Bedside Commodes in 2026
metaDescription: Six drop-arm bedside commodes compared by arm release, padding, seat height, arm spacing and weight rating, for side transfers from a bed or wheelchair.
introParagraphs: Fixed armrests are a help for standing and a barrier for sliding. A person who moves from a wheelchair or a bed to a commode by sliding sideways has to get past the arm, and a caregiver steadying them has to reach around it. A drop-arm commode solves that by letting one or both armrests lower out of the way with a button press, and then lock back up for support. The mechanism is the feature to test, because an arm that sticks or does not lock is a hazard.

The six picks here all have drop arms. The DMI releases both arms on a 500 lb frame, the VOCIC adds adjustable arm spacing and a motion light, the Medline Drop Arm has padded drop-down arms and a foam seat, and the Medline Adjustable Steel gives a published 20-inch gap between the arms. The ProBasics folds and adjusts in one-inch steps, and the Farnuvo gives independent push-button legs and a tall splash guard.

We evaluated each from listing specs and buyer feedback, not from hands-on lab work. For a drop-arm commode, the details we weigh most are how the arm releases and locks, how the seat height compares with the surface the user is transferring from, and how much room is left between the arms once the commode is in place.

products.name: DMI Drop Arm Portable Toilet Commode, 500 lb
products.description:
The DMI has a release button that drops the armrests on both sides for sliding access, on a frame rated to 500 lb. The listing gives overall dimensions of 29.5 by 20.5 by 29.25 inches and a seat of 23.25 by 18.5 inches with adjustable legs giving a height of 20 to 24 inches. The seat is wide, the feet are non-slip and the arm rests are comfortable.

Both arms drop, which is useful if the commode is placed with either side facing the bed, or if the user transfers from different surfaces on different days. The five-liter bucket has a snap-on lid and a carry handle, and lifts out for emptying and rinsing with mild soap and water. The height range starts at 20 inches, higher than some competitors.

It sits in the upper-middle of the price range. Compared with the Medline steel commode it has a higher rating and a wider seat but a smaller bucket. Choose it for a wide, high-rated commode with arms that drop on both sides. Practice releasing and raising both arms with a helper before the first night, and set the height with the user seated. Rinse the bucket promptly and wipe the wide seat dry.
products.bestFor: Larger users and homes where either side of the commode may face the bed.

products.name: VOCIC Drop Arm Bedside Commode with Extra Wide Seat
products.description:
The VOCIC lets you adjust the space between the arms from 18.9 to 22.8 inches and the seat height from 18 to 23 inches. Either armrest flips up with the press of a button, opening the side for transfers and giving caregivers clearer access, and the reinforced steel frame uses dual support bars for a stated 400 lb. A 30 mm padded seat and backrest add comfort.

Adjustable arm spacing is unusual on a drop-arm commode and helps match different bodies and different transfer sizes. A removable waterproof pouch holds toilet paper and small items, and a contoured bucket with a lid lifts out by its handle. The three-mode motion light, off, motion sensor or always on, lights the floor around the commode at night.

It sits in the middle of the price range. Compared with the DMI it adds spacing adjustment and a light but a lower rating. Choose it when width flexibility and night visibility matter. Set the arm spacing to the user first, then the height, and try the motion light in the dark. Empty the side pouch before wiping, and keep the contoured bucket rinsed and dry.
products.bestFor: Users who need adjustable width and a light for night transfers.

products.name: Medline Drop Arm Commode with Padded Seat and Backrest
products.description:
The Medline Drop Arm pads the armrests as well as the seat. Padded drop-down armrests lower for lateral transfers on and off the commode, which the listing describes as ideal for individuals in wheelchairs, and the thick foam seat and removable backrest are comfortable for adults and the elderly. The steel frame is rated to 350 lb, and height adjusts by push button from 18 to 22 inches.

A padded arm is gentler on the forearm and hand when the user pushes up, and a lower height range of 18 to 22 inches matches many wheelchair and bed surfaces. The commode comes with a removable 7.5 qt bucket, lid and splash guard, a clip-on seat that comes off for cleaning, and it works as a raised toilet seat when the bucket and backrest are removed.

It sits in the lower-middle of the price range. Compared with the DMI it has padding on the arms but a lower rating. Choose it for padded arms and a low height range. Check that the padded arm locks firmly each time you raise it, and set the height with push buttons on both sides. Wipe the foam seat and arm pads dry after use.
products.bestFor: Users who want padded drop arms and a seat height near wheelchair level.
pros: Thick foam seat and removable backrest
7.5 qt bucket with lid and splash guard
cons: Does not state width between the arms in the material we reviewed

products.name: Medline Adjustable Steel Drop-Arm Bedside Commode, 350 lb
products.description:
This Medline gives clear numbers. The listing publishes a seat height of 19 to 23 inches, a seat depth of 16.5 inches, an overall width of 23 inches and a 20-inch width between the arms, on a powder-coated steel frame rated to 350 lb. The drop arms assist patients and mobility-impaired individuals in and out, and the commode can be used bedside, as a raised seat over the toilet or, without the seat, as safety rails around the toilet.

Tool-free assembly, easy push-button height adjustment, a convenient toilet paper holder and non-slip rubber feet round it out, with a removable 7.5 qt bucket. The listing notes that disposable liners are sold separately. It is a straightforward, well-documented steel commode with no padding on the seat.

It sits in the lower part of the price range. Compared with the padded Medline it is plainer and cheaper. Choose it for a clearly specified, no-frills drop-arm commode. Measure the transfer surface before ordering, since the listing's numbers make that easy, and test the arm release with the commode empty. Wipe the steel and seat dry and rinse the bucket after use.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want published dimensions and a plain steel drop-arm commode.
pros: Published 20 inch gap between the arms

products.name: ProBasics Drop Arm Adjustable Bedside Folding Commode Chair
products.description:
The ProBasics combines a push-button drop arm with a folding frame. The easy-release arm mechanism allows lateral transfers to and from the commode, soft rubber armrests are anti-slip, and the tool-free removable backrest lets the frame be configured as a bedside commode, a toilet safety frame or a raised toilet seat. Seat height adjusts in one-inch increments, and the frame is rated to 300 lb.

Folding makes the commode easy to store or move, which matters for a household that uses it for a limited period. The 7.5 qt commode bucket slides into place with a carry handle and a splash guard, and the frame is white with gray accessories. The 300 lb rating is the lowest in the group, which suits lighter users.

It sits in the lower-middle of the price range. Compared with the Medline steel commode it folds but has a lower rating. Choose it for a lighter user who needs a drop arm and a folding frame. Fold and unfold it a few times to feel how the frame locks, and test the arm release before relying on it. Wipe the rubber armrests dry and store the frame flat and dry.
products.bestFor: Lighter users who need a drop arm and a commode that folds.
cons: 300 lb capacity is the lowest here

products.name: Farnuvo Drop Arm Bedside Commode Chair
products.description:
The Farnuvo's arm folds down completely, which the listing says lets users slide directly from a wheelchair or bed onto the seat without standing or turning. Thick cushioned padding on the seat and backrest reduces pressure, and each leg has an independent push-button height adjustment with six settings from 19 to 25 inches. The frame is reinforced steel tubing with anti-loosening screws, static tested to 350 lb.

Independent leg adjustment lets you level the commode on a floor that is not perfectly flat, which a single-lever system cannot. The front splash guard is raised higher than most standard models, and the smooth, rounded bucket removes from the rear with one hand. It works bedside, over the toilet or as a shower chair per the listing.

It sits in the middle of the price range. Compared with the VOCIC it has a taller splash guard and leg leveling but no adjustable arm spacing or light. Choose it for leveling and splash protection. Adjust each leg separately until the commode sits flat, then test the arm and the splash guard. Wipe the cushioned seat dry and rinse the rounded bucket after each use.
products.bestFor: Uneven floors and users who want extra splash protection.
pros: Independent leg adjustment from 19 to 25 inches
cons: Seat padding thickness not stated in the material we reviewed

buyingCriteria.criterion: How the arm releases and locks
buyingCriteria.explanation: Most drop arms use a release button that you press, and then the arm swings down and locks back up. The Farnuvo's arm folds down completely, the DMI drops both arms and the ProBasics uses an easy-release push button. Test the mechanism with the commode empty, and make sure the arm locks firmly in the raised position before anyone leans on it. A sticking arm should stop the use of the commode. Ask a helper to try the release on a quiet day, not at the moment of need.

For a side slide, the commode seat should be at or just below the height of the bed or wheelchair seat. The Medline Drop Arm runs 18 to 22 inches, the VOCIC 18 to 23, the Medline steel 19 to 23 and the Farnuvo 19 to 25. Measure the surface the user is moving from and choose a range that brackets it. A seat that is much higher or lower turns a slide into a lift. Match the seat to the surface the user moves from, not to a general number.

The Medline steel publishes 20 inches between the arms, the VOCIC adjusts from 18.9 to 22.8 and the DMI has a 23.25 inch seat. Too narrow a gap is uncomfortable, and too wide a gap reduces the support of the arms when raised. Measure hip width while seated and add room. Adjustable spacing helps if more than one person will use it. If the user is between two widths, choose the one that gives room.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Padding on the seat and arms
buyingCriteria.explanation: The Medline Drop Arm pads the arms and seat, the VOCIC has a 30 mm seat, the Farnuvo a cushioned seat and the Medline steel and ProBasics have firmer surfaces. Padded arms are gentler on the forearm, and a padded seat helps longer sits. Choose firm surfaces if you want the easiest cleaning, and padded ones if comfort matters. If you transfer sideways, padding on the arm is a comfort that you will notice every time.

The DMI states 500 lb, the VOCIC 400 lb, the Medline models and Farnuvo 350 lb and the ProBasics 300 lb. A drop-arm commode loads the frame differently during a slide, so leave margin. Follow the maker's instructions and use the commode on a level floor. Check any rating against the user's weight with margin, and use the commode on a level floor.

A removable bucket with a lid and a splash guard is standard, but details differ: the Farnuvo's taller guard, the VOCIC's contoured bucket and the Medline's clip-on seat. The VOCIC's motion light helps at night. Think about who will empty the bucket and in what light. A motion light only helps if the path to the commode is clear.

howWeEvaluated.title: Arm mechanism
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the DMI's two-sided release, the Farnuvo's fully folding arm, the ProBasics' push-button release and the padded arms on the Medline Drop Arm. Mechanisms that are described clearly scored higher. A clear description of the arm mechanism made it easier to judge the risk.

howWeEvaluated.title: Height and transfer fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We read seat height ranges from 18 to 25 inches and compared them to typical bed and wheelchair surfaces. Lower ranges suit lower surfaces. A seat range that brackets a typical bed is more useful than a wide range.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spacing and comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the VOCIC's adjustable 18.9 to 22.8 inch spacing, the Medline's 20 inch gap and the DMI's wide seat, and at padding on seats and arms. Spacing numbers were treated as part of safety, not just comfort.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We recorded ratings from 300 to 500 lb and noted which listings say the frame was static tested. Static testing claims were noted but not treated as proof.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hygiene and extras
howWeEvaluated.description: We read bucket details, splash guards, pouches and the VOCIC's motion light. Night details counted for more than extras that are used rarely.

howToChoose.intro: Match the seat range to what the user moves from.

faq.q: What is a drop-arm commode for?
faq.a: It lets one or both armrests lower out of the way so a user can slide in from the side, as from a wheelchair or bed. The arms then lock back up for support. It suits users who cannot stand and turn.

faq.q: How do I test the arm release?
faq.a: With the commode empty, press the release button, lower the arm and raise it again, checking that it locks firmly each time. Do it in daylight with the helper present. If the arm sticks, wobbles or fails to lock, do not use it.

faq.q: What seat height is best for a side transfer?
faq.a: The commode seat should be at or slightly below the bed or wheelchair seat. Measure the surface and compare with the commode's range. A seat that is too high makes the slide a climb.

faq.q: Do both arms need to drop?
faq.a: Only if either side might face the bed or the wheelchair. The DMI and VOCIC drop either arm. If the layout is fixed, one drop arm may be enough.

faq.q: Can I use a drop-arm commode over a toilet?
faq.a: Many can, with the bucket removed, but check the arm spacing and height range against your toilet. The Medline steel commode lists use as a raised seat or safety rails. Test the fit first.

faq.q: How do I keep it from moving during a transfer?
faq.a: Place it on a flat, dry floor with the feet seated, lock the legs and ask a helper to steady it for the first practice. The Farnuvo's independent leg adjustment helps on uneven floors. Never transfer to an unsteady commode.

faq.q: Should I ask a professional before buying a drop-arm commode?
faq.a: If the user transfers with difficulty, an occupational therapist can watch a real transfer and recommend arm style, seat height and placement. Bring the measurements of the bed or wheelchair and the commode listing. They can also help choose between a drop-arm commode and other aids.
